Apple scab: symptoms and control

By Gafar Laiya, Gujarat Bio Organics · Updated 2026-11-25

Apple scab, caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis, shows as velvety olive-green spots on leaves and fruit that turn into dark, corky, cracked scabs. It is prevented, not cured: a 5% urea spray on leaves in October speeds the rotting of fallen leaves where the fungus survives winter, and fungicides from different groups are rotated through spring (SKUAST-K 2026).

Symptoms

  • Velvety olive-green spots on young leaves from green tip onwards.
  • Spots darken; leaves curl and fall early.
  • Fruit get dark, corky, scabby patches that crack and lose market value.

Why it keeps coming back

The fungus survives winter in fallen scabbed leaves and releases spores in spring rain from green tip onwards. Orchards that leave last year's leaves on the ground carry the disease forward.

Control

  1. October–November: 5% urea spray on leaves before they fall, then rake or rot fallen leaves.
  2. From green tip in wet weather: protect with fungicides rotated between groups. The SKUAST-K 2026 schedule lists captan, mancozeb, dodine, difenoconazole and myclobutanil; use doses and intervals from the current schedule and label. Do not rely on carbendazim alone.
  3. Keep the canopy open so leaves dry quickly.
  4. In Kashmir, consider scab-resistant Shireen and Firdous.

Pesticide safety: Use only pesticides registered for apple by CIB&RC, at the dose and waiting period on the label, and follow your state's current spray schedule (SKUAST-K, Dr. YSP UHF or the state horticulture department).

Questions farmers ask

What is apple scab?

A fungal disease (Venturia inaequalis) that causes olive spots and corky scabs on apple leaves and fruit.

How do I stop apple scab?

Spray 5% urea on leaves in October to rot fallen leaves, and rotate fungicides from different groups from green tip in wet weather as per the SKUAST-K schedule.

Which apple varieties resist scab?

Shireen and Firdous, released for Kashmir, were bred for scab resistance.
